Consider the region $D$ shown above. If $R=[-2,2]\times [-2,2],$ and

$$
{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

which of the following could be the definition of $f(x,y)?$

I. $\{\begin{aligned}y-x, & (x,y)\in R \\ 0, & (x,y)\notin R\end{aligned}$

II. $\{\begin{aligned}0, & (x,y)\in R∖D \\ y-x, & (x,y)\in D\end{aligned}$

III. $\{\begin{aligned}y-x, & (x,y)\in R∖D, \\ 0, & (x,y)\in D∖R\end{aligned}$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our region $D$ and the rectangle $R:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14157763/assets/976dc1b0a7298c5cf0a331acb00594c8e4c74a14b6df3fc18f7e7997db2956c4.png)

Notice that the rectangle $R$ contains the region $D$ completely. 

Now, if we define $f(x,y)$ to be equal $y-x$ on $D$ and to be equal $0$ outside $D,$ we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given functions.

- We cannot use functions I and III. Both of these functions are not identically zero for all points in $R\,∖D.$ For example, $(x,y)=(2,0)\in R\,∖\,D,$ but the functions are nonzero at this point.

- Function II equals $y-x$ on $D$ and equals $0$ outside $D.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
